title: Beha'alotcha: seventy elders (Numbers 11:16–29)
hookLine: Moses shares the load and says "would that all the LORD's people were prophets"

cards: Every office has one: the person who does everything.

They answer every email, fix every crisis, carry the whole project in their head, until one afternoon they sit in the car in the parking lot and can't make themselves go in. Moses hits that wall in Numbers eleven.

A whole people is weeping for meat at their tent doors, and he turns to God and says something close to: did I give birth to these people? Am I supposed to carry them like a nurse carries a baby? I can't do this alone.

teach.b: God's answer isn't a pep talk. It's a reorganization. Gather seventy of the elders, God says.
I'll take some of the spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they'll carry the burden of the people with you, so you don't carry it alone.

Moses gathers them around the tent of meeting, the spirit rests on them, and they prophesy. But two men named on the list, Eldad and Medad, stayed back in the camp, and the spirit rests on them there too.
They prophesy in the middle of the camp, outside the official circle. A young man runs to tell Moses. Joshua, Moses' loyal assistant, is alarmed: my lord Moses, stop them.
Moses answers: are you jealous for my sake? "would that all the LORD'S people were prophets, that the LORD would put His spirit upon them!" Moses does two things here.

He shares the load: seventy now carry what one was crushing under. And he shares the credit, more than shares it. Two unauthorized prophets in the camp aren't a threat to him; he wishes everyone had what they have.
Later Jewish tradition saw the beginnings of the great court here: seventy elders plus Moses, seventy-one, the number of the Sanhedrin.

teach.h: ELDAD AND MEDAD, IN THE CAMP.
teach.b: But the line that lasts is Moses' wish.

teach.h: ARE YOU JEALOUS FOR MY SAKE?
teach.b: A leader who wants everyone to have the spirit isn't diminished by it.

how: Jewish tradition reads the seventy elders as a root of shared leadership, and the Mishnah links the great court of seventy-one, the Sanhedrin, to Moses and the seventy; Moses' answer to Joshua is often quoted as a model of a leader without jealousy.

o: when you raise up: the portion of the lamps and elders
the seventy elders who sat as Israel's court
the tent where Moses met God outside the camp

games.q: sharing the spirit — tap the pairs.

s: Moses ordered Eldad and Medad to stop
he asked Joshua, are you jealous for my sake? and wished all were prophets.
Moses told God the people were too heavy for him alone
and God answered with seventy elders to share the load.
Eldad and Medad prophesied inside the circle at the tent
they stayed in the camp, and the spirit rested on them there.

games.q: you're Moses. Joshua runs up: two men are prophesying in the camp, outside the official circle. stop them! what do you say?
o: bring them to me at once.
are you jealous for my sake? would that all were prophets.
games.why: Moses isn't threatened. "would that all the LORD'S people were prophets." he shares the load and the credit.

practice: Look at what you carry alone that someone else could hold a corner of, a chore, a worry, the care of an aging parent, and name one person who could take it.
Then look the other way: is someone doing well, maybe outside the official circle, whose success you've quietly guarded against? Picture saying, good for you, I wish more of us could.

wordCard.voice: Beha'alotcha, the portion where Moses, overwhelmed, shares his spirit with seventy elders, and wishes it on everyone.

orig.note: Hebrew: seventy elders. zaken, elder, is related to zakan, beard.

carryVoice: Your line: would all were prophets. Seventy carried what one could not. Four hundred forty-four days now.

sources.q: would that all the LORD'S people were prophets, that the LORD would put His spirit upon them!
